criteria: explains composite index (A, B, C) is sorted primarily by A, then by B within equal A, then by C within equal (A, B)
explains why queries filtering only on B or C cannot perform standard index range scans because B values are scattered across different A subtrees
defines Index Skip Scan: optimizer skips across distinct values of prefix column A to evaluate predicates on subsequent columns
specifies prerequisite for an effective skip scan: leading column A must have very low cardinality (e.g. gender or boolean status) relative to total rows

questions.question: Describe a concrete doctor on-call scheduling scenario where Snapshot Isolation permits a Write Skew anomaly, and explain how to prevent it.
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: sets up the rule: hospital requires at least one doctor on-call at all times; currently Doctors A and B are on call
shows concurrent transactions: T1 reads count=2 and updates A to inactive; T2 concurrently reads count=2 and updates B to inactive
explains why Snapshot Isolation commits both transactions: neither modified the other's row, leaving zero doctors on call
provides solutions: upgrading to true Serializable isolation or using explicit pessimistic locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE)

questions.question: How do relational databases handle tuple versioning under MVCC, and what operational problems arise if dead tuple cleanup fails?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains row header metadata: xmin records creation transaction ID, xmax records deletion/expiration transaction ID
explains that updates create a new tuple version and mark the old tuple version as dead once no active transaction can see it
describes consequences of delayed garbage collection (e.g. failing autovacuum): severe disk bloat, index bloat, and cache degradation
warns about transaction ID wraparound failure if freezing old transaction IDs is neglected

questions.question: In multi-granularity locking, what is a Shared Intent Exclusive (SIX) lock, and what exact transaction operation warrants acquiring it on a table?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines SIX lock as combining the semantics of Shared (S) and Intent Exclusive (IX) at the table level
explains it allows the holder to read all rows of the table while explicitly locking specific individual rows in Exclusive (X) mode for updates
identifies the canonical operation: a transaction that scans the entire table and conditionally updates a small subset of records
describes compatibility: other transactions can only acquire IS locks; they cannot acquire S, IX, or X locks on the SIX-locked table

questions.question: How do the Wait-Die and Wound-Wait deadlock prevention algorithms use transaction timestamps to break circular wait, and which one is preemptive?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains Wait-Die (non-preemptive): if older transaction requests lock held by younger, it waits; if younger requests lock held by older, younger dies (aborts)
explains Wound-Wait (preemptive): if older requests lock held by younger, older wounds (preempts and aborts) younger; if younger requests lock held by older, younger waits
identifies Wound-Wait as preemptive because an older transaction immediately evicts the younger holder
explains that retaining original timestamps upon transaction restart prevents starvation in both schemes

questions.question: Why can standard row-level locks not prevent phantom read anomalies, and what mechanism does the database use instead?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains that row locks only attach to records that physically exist in the database at the time of query execution
points out that a concurrent transaction inserting a brand-new row within the range cannot be blocked by existing row locks
introduces predicate locking (locking all potential records satisfying a predicate)
explains practical index-range locks (Gap Locking and Next-Key Locking) implemented by production engines like MySQL InnoDB

questions.question: What happens internally when a secondary index is searched versus a clustered index in terms of disk I/O and pointer chasing?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains a clustered index leaf node contains the complete physical row data, needing only one B+ tree traversal
explains a secondary index leaf node contains only indexed columns plus a row locator (RID or primary key value)
describes double traversal (bookmark lookup / key lookup): traversing secondary index B+ tree then clustered index B+ tree
contrasts random disk I/O implications between the two lookup patterns

questions.question: What is a covering index, and why does it drastically reduce disk page reads in high-throughput workloads?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines a covering index as an index that contains all columns requested by a query (in SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, and ORDER BY)
explains index-only scans: the database engine satisfies the query entirely from index leaf pages without accessing table pages
explains how this eliminates expensive random table lookups and cache misses
mentions composite indexing or the INCLUDE clause (non-key columns in index leaves) to create covering indexes without bloating the B+ tree search key

questions.question: What is the fundamental structural difference between row-oriented and column-oriented database storage engines?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains row stores write complete tuples contiguously on data pages, ideal for OLTP point lookups and writes
explains column stores write all values of a single attribute contiguously, ideal for OLAP aggregations across few columns
contrasts I/O efficiency: column store avoids reading unreferenced columns into memory during analytical queries
mentions high compression efficiency in columnar stores due to homogenous data types

questions.question: What is a database buffer pool, and why is it essential for disk-based DBMS architectures?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines the buffer pool as a dedicated region of main memory caching database pages read from persistent disk
explains the primary purpose: caching hot pages to avoid orders-of-magnitude slower disk I/O latency
describes how frames hold in-memory copies of disk pages along with dirty and pin metadata
contrasts database buffer management with OS page caching

questions.question: How does a slotted page architecture organize variable-length tuple records inside a physical database page?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains the layout: page header and slot array grow from the start of the page forward, while tuple data grows from the end of the page backward
describes the slot array entry as containing (offset, length) pointing to the physical record location
explains that Record IDs (RIDs) point to page ID and slot number rather than physical byte offsets
highlights that record lengths can vary and data can be defragmented without changing external tuple IDs

questions.question: What is the role of query parsing and semantic analysis (binding) before query optimization?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains parsing converts raw SQL text into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) while verifying syntactic grammar
explains semantic analysis (binding/resolution) checks the system catalog to verify tables, columns, and functions exist
verifies user authorization and access privileges for referenced relations
checks data type compatibility and performs implicit type coercions

questions.question: What is the core difference between a Rule-Based Optimizer (RBO) and a Cost-Based Optimizer (CBO)?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines RBO as relying on static heuristic rules (e.g., always prefer an index scan over full table scan) regardless of data distribution
defines CBO as using mathematical cost models and catalog statistics (cardinality, page counts, histograms) to estimate execution costs
explains why RBO produces sub-optimal execution plans when table cardinalities or filtering selectivities skew
identifies that modern enterprise databases exclusively rely on Cost-Based Optimization

questions.question: What is a bitmap index, and for which types of data attributes is it most effective?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines a bitmap index as storing a bit vector for each distinct column value where each bit position corresponds to a table row
identifies ideal attributes: low-cardinality columns (e.g., gender, marital status, state codes)
explains how boolean queries (AND, OR, NOT) are executed with lightning-fast bitwise hardware CPU instructions
points out the severe drawback: high write/update overhead due to locking entire bit vectors

questions.question: What is a partial index in SQL, and what storage and performance benefits does it provide?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines a partial index as an index built only over a subset of rows satisfying a specific predicate filter
illustrates with a practical example (e.g., indexing only active orders WHERE status = 'PENDING')
explains benefits: significantly smaller index tree size, reduced disk space, and higher cache residency
explains write performance benefit: updates or inserts on rows outside the filter bypass index maintenance entirely

questions.question: What is an expression-based index, and why won't standard indexes optimize queries with functions in the WHERE clause?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains that standard B+ tree indexes store raw column values and cannot evaluate function outputs without row-by-row invocation
shows that queries like WHERE LOWER(username) = 'alice' force full table scans on standard indexes
defines expression-based indexes as pre-computing and indexing the result of an expression or function
explains that query optimizers match the AST expression in the query with the indexed expression definition

questions.question: How does a standard Nested Loop Join algorithm operate, and what is its computational complexity?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains the algorithm: for each tuple in the outer relation R, scan the inner relation S to find matching tuples
states the time complexity without indexes as O(|R| * |S|) comparisons and disk scans
explains Index Nested Loop Join where an index on the inner relation reduces inner lookup complexity to O(|R| * log |S|)
identifies that optimizers prefer the smaller table as the outer driving table

questions.question: What is a dirty page in the buffer pool, and when does it get flushed to disk?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines a dirty page as an in-memory page that has been modified by a transaction but not yet written back to persistent storage
explains flushing triggers: background checkpointing, buffer pool eviction under memory pressure, or clean shutdown
highlights the Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) invariant: corresponding log records must be flushed before the dirty data page reaches disk
contrasts with clean pages which can be discarded instantly without disk writes

questions.question: What information does an EXPLAIN query plan provide to database engineers, and how does it help identify performance bottlenecks?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains EXPLAIN displays the execution plan chosen by the optimizer without running the query (estimated cost, row counts)
explains EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query and returns true execution times, loops, and actual row counts
identifies access method indicators: Sequential Scan vs Index Scan vs Index-Only Scan
highlights how comparing estimated rows against actual rows reveals stale catalog statistics

questions.question: What is an inverted index, and how does it power full-text search engines?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines an inverted index as mapping distinct words/tokens to a postings list of document IDs and positions containing them
contrasts with forward index (which maps documents to their containing words)
explains the text processing pipeline: tokenization, stop-word removal, and stemming/lemmatization
explains how multi-term boolean queries intersect or union individual postings lists

questions.question: What is the operational distinction between running VACUUM and running ANALYZE on a PostgreSQL table?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains VACUUM cleans up dead row versions left by MVCC updates/deletes and marks space reusable in the free space map
explains ANALYZE samples table rows to collect distribution statistics (histograms, most common values, null fractions) for the query optimizer
points out that running VACUUM without ANALYZE reclaims disk space but does not update optimizer statistics
points out that running ANALYZE does not clean up dead rows or shrink table bloat

questions.question: How does the Clock page replacement algorithm approximate LRU in buffer pool management with lower lock contention?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains the circular buffer layout with a sweeping clock hand pointer and a reference/usage bit for each frame
describes hit handling: when a page is accessed, its reference bit is set to 1 without acquiring global linked-list mutexes
describes eviction pass: hand checks bit; if 1, clears to 0 and advances; if 0 (and unpinned), page is selected for eviction
explains why Clock scales better than exact LRU under multi-threaded concurrency

questions.question: What is sequential scan flooding (buffer pool pollution), and how do algorithms like 2Q or LRU-K mitigate it?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines pollution: a single large sequential table scan reads gigabytes of cold pages, evicting all hot frequently accessed pages from LRU cache
explains the limitation of standard LRU: treats a page read once during a table scan as most-recently-used
explains LRU-K: tracks the timestamp of the last K accesses, requiring multiple references before promoting a page into hot cache
explains 2Q: uses a FIFO queue for newly loaded pages and only moves pages to a main LRU queue upon subsequent re-reference

questions.question: In database recovery and buffer management, what is the difference between a Steal policy and a No-Steal policy?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Steal: the buffer pool manager is permitted to write dirty pages modified by uncommitted transactions to disk to free frames
defines No-Steal: pages modified by active uncommitted transactions must remain in RAM until commit
explains trade-offs: Steal maximizes buffer pool utilization for large transactions exceeding RAM, but requires UNDO logging for crash recovery
explains No-Steal simplifies recovery (no undo needed) but artificially caps transaction write sets to available memory

questions.question: What is the difference between a Force and a No-Force buffer flushing policy, and why do modern high-performance databases use No-Force?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Force: all modified data pages must be physically flushed to disk before a transaction can successfully commit
defines No-Force: transaction can commit as soon as its log records are flushed to WAL, leaving dirty data pages in RAM
explains why Force causes terrible random I/O write bottlenecks and latency spikes on rotational and flash media
explains that No-Force enables sequential WAL append and deferred background dirty page flushing at the cost of requiring REDO recovery

questions.question: What are the core architectural components of a Log-Structured Merge-tree, and why is it optimized for write-heavy workloads?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies four core components: Write-Ahead Log (WAL), in-memory MemTable, Bloom Filters, and disk-based Sorted String Tables (SSTables)
explains write path: incoming writes append sequentially to WAL for durability and insert into in-memory sorted MemTable (SkipList/rbtree)
explains why it is write-optimized: converts all random write operations into sequential disk I/O flushes
contrasts write performance against B+ trees which require random in-place page writes

questions.question: How does an LSM-tree transition data from volatile memory to immutable disk files?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains that when the active MemTable reaches its memory threshold, it is switched to an immutable (read-only) MemTable
describes how a new active MemTable is allocated immediately so incoming writes never stall
describes background flushing: a worker thread iterates through the sorted immutable MemTable and writes an SSTable to Level 0 disk storage
explains that after SSTable flush completion, the associated WAL segment is safely truncated and the immutable MemTable freed

questions.question: How do Bloom filters prevent unnecessary disk I/O lookups for non-existent keys in LSM-tree storage engines?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines a Bloom filter as a space-efficient probabilistic data structure using k hash functions over an m-bit array
highlights the guarantee: zero false negatives (if Bloom filter says NO, the key definitely does not exist in the SSTable)
explains how it handles false positives: if filter says YES, engine reads SSTable, occasionally finding key is absent
shows that reading SSTables on disk is skipped for negative filter hits, drastically accelerating point reads

questions.question: What is the difference between Size-Tiered Compaction Strategy and Leveled Compaction Strategy in LSM-tree engines?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains STCS groups SSTables of similar sizes together and merges them into a larger SSTable, optimizing for write-heavy workloads
explains LCS divides disk storage into levels (L0, L1, L2...) where each level is 10x larger and SSTables within L1+ have strictly non-overlapping key ranges
contrasts space amplification: STCS requires up to 50% free disk headroom for compaction, whereas LCS maintains low space amplification (~10%)
contrasts read performance: LCS guarantees at most one SSTable read per level for point lookups

questions.question: How does a Block Nested Loop join reduce disk page transfers compared to a naive nested loop join?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies flaw of naive nested loop: for every single tuple in the outer table, the entire inner table is read from disk
explains BNL approach: loads a large chunk (block of memory frames) of outer table tuples into RAM
scans the inner table once per outer block rather than once per outer tuple
compares I/O formulas: O(|R| + (|R|/B) * |S|) page transfers instead of O(|R| + |R| * |S|)

questions.question: How does the classic in-memory Hash Join algorithm execute its Build and Probe phases?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies prerequisite: applies exclusively to equi-joins (equality join predicates)
defines Build Phase: scans the smaller relation (build input) and populates an in-memory hash table hashed on join keys
defines Probe Phase: scans the larger relation (probe input), hashes each tuple's join key, and checks hash table buckets for matching tuples
states optimal time complexity: O(|R| + |S|) time

questions.question: How does a Grace Hash Join handle datasets where the hash build table exceeds available RAM?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains Partitioning Phase: hashes both relations R and S into matching bucket pairs on disk using hash function h1
explains matching partitions rule: tuple in partition R_i can only join with tuple in partition S_i
explains Join Phase: loads each R_i partition into memory and builds hash table using a secondary hash function h2, then probes with S_i
describes recursive partitioning if individual partitions still exceed memory buffer size

questions.question: When does a query optimizer select a Sort-Merge Join over a Hash Join, and how does it leverage sorted inputs?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains the two steps: sorting both relations on join attributes (if not already ordered), then concurrently scanning and merging matches like merge-sort
explains optimizer preference: when inputs are already sorted by an index or prior ORDER BY clause ('interesting orders')
contrasts with Hash Join: Sort-Merge works for inequality range joins (<, <=, >, >=) while Hash Join requires strict equality
notes that Sort-Merge Join outputs results in sorted order without requiring an extra sorting node

questions.question: How do database statistics and histograms influence cardinality estimation in cost-based query optimization?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines cardinality estimation as predicting the number of rows that will satisfy filter and join predicates
explains how naive uniform distribution assumptions produce catastrophic estimation errors on skewed datasets
explains how histograms record frequency distribution across buckets to compute realistic selectivity
shows how incorrect cardinality leads optimizers to pick disastrous join algorithms or suboptimal join orderings

questions.question: What is the difference between equi-depth and equi-width histograms in database catalog statistics?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Equi-Width: divides attribute value domain into intervals of equal range width; number of tuples per bucket varies
defines Equi-Depth (Equi-Height): divides domain such that each bucket contains approximately the same number of rows; bucket interval widths vary
explains why Equi-Depth is vastly superior for skewed data distributions
identifies that modern enterprise databases like PostgreSQL and Oracle use equi-depth histograms combined with Most Common Values (MCV) lists

questions.question: What is the fill factor of a B+ tree index, and how does configuring it prevent premature page splits during frequent insertions?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines fill factor as the percentage of space on each index leaf page allocated for data during index creation or rebuild
explains why a 100% fill factor causes immediate, costly page splits upon subsequent random inserts
explains how setting a lower fill factor (e.g. 70-80%) reserves free space on leaf pages to absorb random inserts smoothly
notes that read-only archive tables should use 100% fill factor to maximize page density and cache residency

questions.question: Under what threshold does a B+ tree node merge with its sibling or redistribute keys, and why do many production databases choose not to merge aggressively?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains classical B+ tree rule: when deletions cause a node to fall below half capacity (50% occupancy), it borrows keys or merges with a sibling
explains why immediate merging causes catastrophic thrashing under alternating insert/delete workloads
identifies that production engines (like PostgreSQL and MySQL InnoDB) delay merging or allow underfilled pages to avoid expensive tree-wide locking and split-merge oscillation
mentions index rebuilds or reindexing as the preferred administrative approach for defragmentation

questions.question: What are the three distinct passes of the ARIES crash recovery algorithm, and what is the goal of each pass?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Analysis Pass: scans log forward from last checkpoint to reconstruct Dirty Page Table (DPT) and Transaction Table (TT) at crash time
defines Redo Pass: repeats history from smallest RecLSN in DPT, reapplying logged changes for all transactions to restore exact pre-crash state
defines Undo Pass: scans log backward reversing updates made by active transactions (losers) that never committed before the crash
connects ARIES to durability and atomicity

questions.question: How do Log Sequence Numbers establish consistency between the WAL and data pages in buffer memory?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines LSN as a monotonically increasing 64-bit integer indexing byte offsets or sequence IDs in the transaction log
defines PageLSN as the LSN of the most recent log record updating that specific physical page
defines FlushedLSN as the largest LSN written safely to non-volatile disk log storage
states the fundamental WAL invariant: PageLSN <= FlushedLSN must hold before a dirty page can be written to disk

questions.question: What is a Compensation Log Record in ARIES recovery, and how does it prevent infinite logging during crashes that occur while rolling back?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines a CLR as a special log record written during the Undo phase to log the undoing of an original update operation
explains the UndoNextLSN pointer: stores a direct pointer to the next undo log record that needs reversing for that transaction
explains scenario: system crashes midway through undo; on reboot, recovery encounters the CLR and resumes directly from UndoNextLSN
explains why CLRs are never themselves undone, guaranteeing that crash recovery work is strictly bounded and monotonic

questions.question: What is write amplification, and why is write amplification typically higher in B+ tree engines than LSM-tree engines?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines write amplification as the ratio of physical bytes written to persistent disk storage divided by logical bytes requested by the application
explains B+ tree write amplification: modifying a 50-byte record requires writing an entire 8KB or 16KB dirty page to disk
explains LSM-tree write path: appends compact delta records sequentially into WAL and memory buffers without writing full pages immediately
connects high write amplification to SSD flash endurance degradation and I/O bottlenecks

questions.question: What causes read amplification in database engines, and why do LSM-tree engines face greater read amplification than B+ trees?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines read amplification as the ratio of bytes read from disk compared to the actual bytes requested by the application
explains B+ tree deterministic lookup: traverse root-to-leaf in O(log N) page reads, reading exactly one leaf page containing the target key
explains LSM read path: key may reside in MemTable, L0 SSTables, or multiple lower levels, requiring checks across multiple files
highlights how Bloom filters and compaction serve as essential mitigations for LSM read amplification

questions.question: What is space amplification, and how do dead tuples and obsolete SSTables contribute to disk space bloat?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines space amplification as the ratio of total physical disk space consumed on media divided by actual active data size
explains how B+ tree fragmentation and deleted row slots remain unused if key distribution is uneven
explains how LSM engines append delete tombstones and update versions, consuming disk space until background compaction cleans them
evaluates operational risks: sudden disk exhaustion caused by delayed vacuuming or compaction backpressure

questions.question: Why does the Redo pass in ARIES recovery repeat history by redoing changes for both committed and active (uncommitted) transactions?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains that redoing changes for uncommitted transactions restores the database buffer and lock state exactly as it existed at the instant of failure
explains why fine-grained concurrency control and page allocation operations require this deterministic state before undo can safely run
shows how repeating history separates page-level structural invariants from transaction-level logical rollback
explains how PageLSN checks make redo actions idempotent: if PageLSN >= LogRecord.LSN, the action is skipped

questions.question: How does a fuzzy checkpoint in ARIES work without freezing active transactions or forcing dirty pages to disk?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: contrasts with hard checkpoints: does not flush all dirty pages and never stalls ongoing transactions
describes two-phase checkpoint logging: writes begin_checkpoint, snapshots current Transaction Table and Dirty Page Table in memory, then writes end_checkpoint
explains RecLSN in DPT: records the earliest log record whose changes have not yet been flushed to disk for that page
explains how fuzzy checkpoints provide the exact minimum starting LSN for the subsequent recovery Redo pass

questions.question: How does a Cost-Based Optimizer use dynamic programming to find the optimal multi-table join order, and why does it struggle beyond 10-12 tables?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains bottom-up DP construction: computes best access path for single tables, then 2-table joins, then memoizes optimal 3-table subplans
explains how optimal substructure allows pruning suboptimal subplans with identical outputs and ordering
analyzes search space explosion: number of join permutations grows as (2N)! / N! for bushy trees and N! for left-deep trees
explains that beyond 10-12 tables, optimizer memory consumption and optimization planning time exceed actual query execution time

questions.question: When multi-table join search spaces become prohibitively large for dynamic programming, how do query optimizers use genetic algorithms?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies trigger: query join threshold exceeded (e.g., geqo_threshold in PostgreSQL, default 12 tables)
explains chromosome encoding: join orders are represented as integer sequences or permutations of relation IDs
describes genetic cycle: initial population generation, fitness evaluation based on estimated cost, crossover, mutation, and survival selection
evaluates trade-offs: achieves near-optimal join plans in bounded O(iterations) time, but sacrifices deterministic reproducibility

questions.question: Compare the traditional Volcano iterator model with vectorized query execution in modern analytical database engines.
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains Volcano iterator model: query tree operators communicate via next() calls producing one single tuple at a time
identifies Volcano flaws: massive virtual function call overhead, poor CPU instruction cache locality, and zero SIMD vectorization
explains Vectorized execution (Block-at-a-time): operators process batches of 1024 or 4096 column vectors per iteration
highlights benefits: high L1/L2 data cache residency, loop unrolling, and hardware SIMD parallelism accelerating filtering and aggregations

questions.question: How do run-length encoding, dictionary encoding, and frame-of-reference compression achieve dramatic space savings in columnar storage engines?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains RLE: replaces contiguous repeating sequences with (value, count) pairs, achieving massive compression on sorted columns
explains Dictionary Encoding: builds an index table of distinct string/complex values and replaces data entries with small 1-2 byte integer IDs
explains Frame of Reference (FoR): subtracts a base minimum value from integer ranges, storing only small relative offsets using minimal bits
shows how query engines execute filtering directly on compressed data without decompression overhead

questions.question: How would you architect a high-frequency financial counter or inventory reservation system to avoid row-level lock serialization on a single database record?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies problem: thousands of concurrent transactions updating the same row (UPDATE balance) block behind a single exclusive row lock
proposes Sharded Counter pattern: splits the single counter into N independent sub-counter rows, where transactions randomly increment one slot
explains total calculation: SUM() across all N slots during balance inquiries
proposes asynchronous memory batching: buffering increments in Redis/Kafka and flushing coalesced deltas periodically to the database

questions.question: How does the Lehman-Yao B-link tree algorithm allow readers and writers to traverse index nodes concurrently without holding read latches during page splits?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies B-link additions: each internal and leaf node contains a right sibling pointer and a 'high key' (upper bound of keys in node)
explains reader traversal: reader descends without holding latches; if target key exceeds node high key, reader follows sibling link to the right
explains split handling: writer creates right sibling and links it before updating the parent node
demonstrates how this eliminates deadlocks between concurrent upward-moving splits and downward-moving searches

questions.question: In relational databases supporting complex JSONB or geometric data, when should an engineer choose a GIN index versus a GiST index?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains GIN (Generalized Inverted Index): maps individual elements/keys to rows, optimal for composite attributes containing multiple values (arrays, JSONB @>)
explains GiST (Generalized Search Tree): balanced tree structure for hierarchical and spatial data (PostGIS bounding boxes, range types, KNN nearest-neighbor)
contrasts write performance: GIN has high update overhead because modifying one row updates multiple inverted index entries
contrasts read performance: GIN provides faster lookups for multi-key lookups, whereas GiST supports complex lossy predicates and spatial indexing

questions.question: How does a database engine partition and execute an analytical aggregation query across multiple worker threads, and how does work-stealing balance thread skew?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains query execution decomposition: query coordinator spawns worker threads, allocating parallel sequential page scans or hash partitions
describes partial aggregation: workers compute intermediate SUM and COUNT locally in parallel without inter-thread locking
describes Gather / Finalize node: coordinator combines partial worker results into the final aggregate output
explains work-stealing: idle threads steal page chunks from queues of slow threads to prevent stragglers from delaying query completion

questions.question: How does WAL Group Commit work, and how does it balance fsync disk latency with high transaction commit throughput?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies bottleneck: calling fsync() to flush the log buffer for every single transaction commit limits throughput to disk IOPS (~200 on HDD, thousands on SSD)
explains Group Commit mechanism: first transaction in queue becomes the Group Leader; subsequent committing transactions register as followers
describes flush execution: leader performs a single fsync() for the entire accumulated batch and wakes up all follower transactions
highlights how group commit scales linearly with concurrency: higher transaction load results in larger batches per fsync

questions.question: How does byte-addressable Non-Volatile Memory reshape database logging and recovery architectures by bypassing traditional WAL pipelines?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains NVM characteristics: combines near-DRAM read/write speeds with persistent data retention, accessible directly via CPU load/store instructions
explains elimination of WAL: allows in-place atomic updates using CPU cache flush (clwb) and memory fences (sfence) without double-writing to disk logs
describes instant recovery: removes minutes-long ARIES log replay because data structures in PMEM remain directly consistent across power loss
identifies hardware challenges: managing pointer validation and memory leaks across system reboots

questions.question: How did the optimization of Common Table Expressions change from being an unconditional optimization fence to being inlined, and how does AS MATERIALIZED affect execution?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains historical behavior: CTEs were treated as black-box optimization fences, materialized completely in temporary buffers preventing predicate pushdown
explains modern behavior (PostgreSQL 12+): non-recursive, side-effect-free CTEs referenced only once are automatically inlined as subqueries
shows how inlining enables cross-CTE join reordering, index selection, and predicate pushdown
explains explicit control: AS MATERIALIZED forces physical materialization (useful for expensive functions or isolating unstable subqueries)

questions.question: How do cache-conscious index architectures align node structures with CPU cache line sizes to eliminate memory bus stalls?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies hardware reality: main memory access is orders of magnitude slower than CPU registers, making L1/L2/L3 cache misses the primary index search bottleneck
explains cache-line alignment: sizes index tree nodes to exact multiples of 64 bytes (cache line size) to prevent single nodes spanning multiple cache lines
explains pointer elimination: arranges nodes in contiguous arrays where child positions are calculated mathematically (implicit pointers like binary heaps)
explains SIMD intra-node searching: compares 4 to 8 keys simultaneously in a single CPU instruction

questions.question: What makes a WHERE predicate Search Argument Able (SARGable), and how does wrapping columns in scalar functions degrade index scans?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines SARGable predicates as conditions formatted such that the query engine can directly utilize a B+ tree index range seek
explains how non-SARGable patterns (e.g. WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2024 or WHERE price * 1.1 > 100) prevent index traversal and force full scans
rewrites non-SARGable predicates into SARGable equivalents (e.g. WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' AND order_date < '2025-01-01')
warns against implicit type conversion (e.g. comparing string column with integer literal) silently nullifying index usability

questions.question: What is a Multivalued Dependency (MVD) in database normalization theory?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines MVD (A ->> B) as asserting that attribute B is independent of other attributes in the relation for a given value of A
explains tuple generation: if tuples (a, b1, c1) and (a, b2, c2) exist, then (a, b1, c2) and (a, b2, c1) must also exist
provides a classic example: an employee having multiple independent hobbies and multiple independent spoken languages
explains that MVDs lead to massive cartesian product redundancy in a single table

questions.question: What condition must a relation satisfy to achieve Fourth Normal Form (4NF)?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: states prerequisite: the relation must already be in Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF)
states the core rule: for every non-trivial multivalued dependency X ->> Y, X must be a superkey
defines a trivial MVD: where Y is a subset of X, or X union Y contains all attributes of the relation
explains how decomposing the relation into two tables eliminates non-trivial MVD redundancy

questions.question: What is the difference between horizontal database sharding and table partitioning?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains table partitioning divides a large table into smaller physical files managed within a single database instance on one server
explains horizontal sharding distributes rows across independent database servers/nodes across a network
contrasts management: partitioning is handled natively by the DBMS storage engine; sharding requires cluster routing or middleware
contrasts scaling limits: partitioning scales vertically up to single-node limits; sharding scales horizontally across nodes

questions.question: How does master-replica database replication operate, and how does it segregate read and write workloads?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains role segregation: the Master (Primary) receives all write transactions (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and records changes to its WAL
describes replication: Replicas (Secondaries) pull WAL changes and apply them locally to maintain up-to-date read-only copies
explains workload distribution: application routes write traffic to primary and balances read-heavy queries across replicas
notes failover mechanisms when the master node crashes

questions.question: What is the core trade-off between synchronous replication and asynchronous replication in database clusters?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains synchronous replication: primary waits for at least one replica to acknowledge log persistence before returning commit success to client
explains asynchronous replication: primary commits locally and confirms to client immediately, transmitting log updates to replicas in background
contrasts latency: asynchronous provides sub-millisecond writes; synchronous incurs round-trip network latency per write
contrasts durability/data loss: asynchronous risks data loss during primary crash; synchronous guarantees zero data loss (RPO = 0)

questions.question: What are the three guarantees of the CAP theorem, and why can a distributed system only guarantee two under a network partition?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Consistency (Linearizability): every read receives the most recent write or an error
defines Availability: every non-failing node returns a non-error response without guaranteeing latest data
defines Partition Tolerance: system continues operating despite arbitrary dropped or delayed network packets between nodes
explains the forced trade-off: network partitions are physical realities, forcing systems to choose between Consistency (CP) or Availability (AP)

questions.question: What do the BASE properties stand for in NoSQL databases, and how do they contrast with ACID?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Basically Available: system guarantees availability by responding to all requests, potentially with degraded or partial data
defines Soft State: data state may change over time without user interaction due to background replica convergence
defines Eventual Consistency: system guarantees all replicas will eventually become consistent if no new updates occur
contrasts with ACID: trades immediate strong consistency and strict isolation for high horizontal availability and partition tolerance

questions.question: What are the three fundamental Armstrong's Axioms used to infer functional dependencies?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Axiom of Reflexivity: If Y is a subset of X, then X -> Y holds
defines Axiom of Augmentation: If X -> Y holds, then XZ -> YZ holds for any attribute set Z
defines Axiom of Transitivity: If X -> Y and Y -> Z hold, then X -> Z holds
states that these three axioms are sound (produce only valid dependencies) and complete (derive all valid dependencies)

questions.question: How does hash-based sharding distribute rows across database nodes, and what is its primary benefit?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains the mechanism: applies a deterministic hash function to the shard key (e.g., hash(user_id) % N) to select target shard node
identifies primary benefit: evenly distributes writes and reads across all cluster nodes, preventing write hotspots
identifies primary limitation: destroys natural key ordering, making range queries require scatter-gather scans across all shards
explains why shard key selection is critical for query routing

questions.question: What is range-based sharding, and what common pitfall causes hotspotting in write workloads?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains range-based sharding assigns contiguous ranges of keys (e.g. A-D on Node 1, E-H on Node 2) to specific nodes
highlights the major advantage: efficient range scans because contiguous rows reside on the same physical shard
identifies the hotspotting trap: sharding on monotonically increasing keys (auto-increment ID, current timestamp)
explains that all current writes hit the single highest-range shard, completely overwhelming one node while others sit idle

questions.question: What is read-after-write consistency, and why do asynchronous replicas frequently violate it?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines read-after-write consistency as guaranteeing that a user who updates data will immediately see that update upon subsequent reads
explains why asynchronous replicas fail this: write commits to primary, user immediately refreshes, read routes to replica where WAL has not yet replayed
illustrates user symptom: user submits comment or updates profile, refreshes page, and data appears reverted or missing
provides mitigations: sticky routing (routing user's own reads to primary for a cooldown window) or tracking client update timestamps

questions.question: What is a split-brain condition in a database cluster, and what catastrophic data corruption can it cause?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines split-brain: a network partition disconnects cluster nodes, causing both isolated partitions to independently elect an active Primary
explains dual-write execution: clients in Partition A write to Leader A; clients in Partition B write conflicting data to Leader B
describes the catastrophic outcome: divergent write histories on identical records that cannot be automatically merged upon network reconnection
explains quorum consensus (requiring strict majority > N/2 votes) as the universal architectural safeguard against split-brain

questions.question: How does an SQL injection attack occur, and why do parameterized queries neutralize it?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains SQL injection: untrusted user input is directly concatenated into SQL strings, altering the abstract syntax tree and executing unauthorized commands
explains prepared statements: the SQL query structure is sent and pre-compiled on the database server with parameter placeholders (?)
explains parameter binding: input parameters are transmitted separately at the protocol level and treated strictly as literal data values
shows that even malicious payloads (e.g. ' OR '1'='1) are interpreted harmlessly as string literals without modifying query logic

questions.question: What are the pros and cons of using a surrogate key versus a natural key as a primary key?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines natural key as an existing real-world attribute uniquely identifying an entity (e.g. SSN, VIN, email)
defines surrogate key as an artificially generated identifier with zero business meaning (e.g. auto-increment INT, UUID)
highlights natural key risks: business requirements change, keys change or suffer typos, triggering expensive cascading foreign key updates
highlights surrogate key advantages: compact immutable integer keys maximizing B+ tree index packing and join performance

questions.question: How do the SQL standard functions COALESCE() and NULLIF() handle NULL values?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines COALESCE(val1, val2, ...): returns the first non-NULL expression from its argument list, returning NULL only if all arguments evaluate to NULL
defines NULLIF(expr1, expr2): returns NULL if both expressions are equal; otherwise returns expr1
illustrates COALESCE practical use: providing fallback values for missing data (e.g. COALESCE(phone, 'N/A'))
illustrates NULLIF practical use: preventing division-by-zero errors (e.g. total / NULLIF(count, 0))

questions.question: What is a Join Dependency, and how does Fifth Normal Form eliminate redundancy beyond 4NF?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Join Dependency *(R1, R2, ... Rn): a relation R can be reconstructed without spurious tuples by joining its projections R1 through Rn
explains 5NF definition: a relation is in 5NF if and only if every non-trivial join dependency is implied by the candidate keys of the relation
illustrates with a 3-way ternary relationship: (Agent, Company, Product) where an agent sells a product only if the company makes that product and agent represents company
explains that 5NF eliminates cyclic join redundancies that cannot be detected by binary functional or multivalued dependencies

questions.question: What is Domain-Key Normal Form (DKNF), and why is it considered the ultimate theoretical normal form?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines DKNF: a relation is in DKNF if every constraint on the relation is a logical consequence of domain constraints and key constraints alone
explains domain constraints (valid data types, ranges, permitted values) and key constraints (uniqueness of candidate keys)
explains theoretical power: a table in DKNF is completely free of all insertion, update, and deletion anomalies
explains practical limitation: no general mechanical algorithm exists to transform an arbitrary schema into DKNF, making it an ideal theoretical target

questions.question: How does the Attribute Closure algorithm determine whether an attribute set forms a superkey or candidate key?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: describes closure computation X+: initialize closure = X; repeatedly add RHS of any FD whose LHS is a subset of current closure until no changes occur
explains superkey test: if X+ contains all attributes of relation R, then X is a valid superkey
explains candidate key test: X is a candidate key if X is a superkey AND no proper subset of X is a superkey (minimality check)
highlights that attribute closure runs in polynomial time, enabling automated schema verification

questions.question: What is a Canonical Cover of a set of functional dependencies, and what are the steps to compute it?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines a canonical cover Fc as an equivalent minimal set of FDs with zero redundant dependencies and zero extraneous attributes
describes step 1: make all RHS singleton attributes using the decomposition rule (e.g. X -> YZ becomes X -> Y and X -> Z)
describes step 2: eliminate extraneous attributes from LHS and RHS of each dependency using closure testing
describes step 3: eliminate redundant functional dependencies that are implied by the remaining dependencies in the set

questions.question: Explain the derived Armstrong's Axioms: Decomposition, Union, and Pseudo-transitivity, and show how they are proven.
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Decomposition: If X -> YZ, then X -> Y and X -> Z (proven via Reflexivity on YZ -> Y and Transitivity)
defines Union: If X -> Y and X -> Z, then X -> YZ (proven via Augmentation of X -> Y with Z to get XZ -> YZ, and Augmentation of X -> Z to get XX -> XZ)
defines Pseudo-transitivity: If X -> Y and WY -> Z, then WX -> Z (proven via Augmentation of X -> Y with W to get WX -> WY, then Transitivity)
shows how derived rules accelerate manual and automated closure computations

questions.question: How do valid-time and transaction-time differ in temporal database tables?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Valid-Time (Application Time): the period during which a fact is true in the real world, managed and assigned by the user/application
defines Transaction-Time (System Time): the period during which a fact is physically stored and recorded in the database, assigned strictly by the DBMS clock
contrasts mutability: valid-time ranges can be modified or backdated retroactively; transaction-time is strictly append-only and immutable
explains why financial and healthcare audit compliance mandates recording both timelines

questions.question: What is a bi-temporal table, and how does it provide full historical auditing and retroactive correction capabilities?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines a bi-temporal table as combining both valid-time intervals [valid_from, valid_to) and transaction-time intervals [system_from, system_to)
explains retroactive correction: adjusting an insurance policy discount rate that should have been active last month without destroying what the database actually believed last month
demonstrates time-travel querying using SQL:2011 standard clauses (FOR PORTION OF BUSINESS_TIME and AS OF SYSTEM TIME)
explains how bi-temporal tables enable recreating the exact database state that generated an audited financial report a year ago

questions.question: How does consistent hashing with virtual nodes minimize data migration during cluster scale-out?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains the hash ring: keys and nodes are hashed onto a circular 2^32 or 2^64 integer space; a key is stored on the first node encountered clockwise
explains the rebalancing advantage: adding or removing a node migrates only K/N keys rather than re-shuffling almost all data under naive hash modulo
defines virtual nodes (vnodes): mapping multiple token points on the ring to a single physical machine
explains how vnodes prevent non-uniform data distribution (clustering) and facilitate proportional capacity allocation for heterogeneous hardware

questions.question: How does semi-synchronous replication operate, and how does it balance write latency with data durability?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains the workflow: primary writes transaction to WAL, ships log to replica, and waits until at least ONE replica writes the log to its relay log disk
explains primary commit: primary proceeds to commit and return success to client without waiting for replica to actually execute/apply the transaction
contrasts with fully synchronous: avoids waiting for all replicas or slow table replaying
contrasts with asynchronous: guarantees that at least one replica has the physical log, preventing data loss during failover

questions.question: What causes database replication lag on read replicas, and what architecture strategies mitigate stale reads?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies root causes: multi-threaded concurrent writes on primary replayed by a single-threaded SQL apply thread on replica, or long read queries blocking replica apply
identifies network latency and disk I/O saturation on replica nodes as major contributors
explains engine solutions: multi-threaded applier (MTS / parallel replication based on write sets or transaction dependency graphs)
explains architectural mitigations: heartbeat monitoring (pt-heartbeat), routing critical reads to primary, or tracking GTID transaction coordinates in client cookies

questions.question: How does the PACELC theorem extend the CAP theorem by describing system behavior under normal operation?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: decodes the acronym: If Partition (P), choose Availability (A) or Consistency (C); Else (E), choose Latency (L) or Consistency (C)
explains CAP theorem flaw: CAP only addresses behavior during rare network partition events, ignoring 99.9% of normal operating time
explains normal operation trade-off: to maintain strong consistency, replicas must coordinate over network, inevitably increasing read/write latency (PC/EC)
classifies real-world databases: MongoDB and Spanner as PC/EC, Cassandra and DynamoDB as PA/EL

questions.question: What are the Prepare and Commit phases of the Two-Phase Commit protocol across distributed database nodes?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Prepare Phase: coordinator sends PREPARE message to all participants; participants acquire locks, write undo/redo logs to persistent disk, and reply VOTE_COMMIT or VOTE_ABORT
defines Commit Phase (success): if all vote COMMIT, coordinator logs COMMIT to WAL and sends GLOBAL_COMMIT; participants commit changes, release locks, and reply ACK
defines Commit Phase (failure): if any participant votes ABORT or times out, coordinator logs ABORT and broadcasts GLOBAL_ABORT to roll back all participants
explains that 2PC guarantees atomic commitment across independent heterogeneous database instances

questions.question: What happens to participant database nodes if the 2PC transaction coordinator crashes during the commit phase?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies the in-doubt window: participant has voted COMMIT during Prepare phase, has locked its local records, and is waiting for coordinator's GLOBAL_COMMIT/ABORT
explains the dilemma: participant cannot unilaterally commit (coordinator might have aborted) and cannot unilaterally abort (coordinator might have committed)
explains blocking failure: participant must hold exclusive resource locks indefinitely until the coordinator recovers
describes severe operational impact: held locks block other concurrent transactions, leading to cluster-wide transaction stalls

questions.question: How does the Three-Phase Commit protocol attempt to remove the blocking coordinator failure vulnerability of 2PC?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies the three phases: Can-Commit? -> Pre-Commit -> Do-Commit
explains Pre-Commit phase: coordinator verifies participants are ready, logs pre-commit, and informs participants before any actual commit occurs
explains timeout handling: if coordinator crashes during Pre-Commit, participants can safely time out and proceed to commit because all voted ready
explains why 3PC is rarely implemented in practice: it requires synchronous networking and fails under network partitions where split-brain can still cause divergence

questions.question: How do distributed databases use Read and Write quorums over N replicas to achieve strong consistency?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines parameters: N = total replica count, W = write quorum (number of replicas that must acknowledge write), R = read quorum (number of replicas read)
explains the mathematical invariant R + W > N: guaranteed overlap of at least one replica between the read set and write set (Pigeonhole Principle)
describes read reconciliation: client queries R replicas, reads version timestamps, and takes the newest value
analyzes trade-offs: lowering W to 1 speeds up writes but sacrifices strong consistency unless R = N

questions.question: How do multi-master database replication topologies detect and resolve concurrent write conflicts on the same record?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies the conflict: Client 1 updates row X on Master A while Client 2 concurrently updates row X on Master B before replication syncs
explains Last-Write-Wins (LWW): uses wall-clock timestamps to overwrite older writes, warning of clock skew silently dropping valid updates
explains Version Vectors / Vector Clocks: detects causal divergence and flags conflicts for deterministic resolution
describes custom resolution strategies: application-defined merge triggers, CRDT data structures, or queuing conflicts in exception tables

questions.question: What are Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types, and how do state-based and operation-based CRDTs guarantee convergence?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines CRDTs as data structures replicated across multiple nodes that can be updated concurrently without central coordination or distributed locks
explains State-based CRDTs (CvRDT): replicas send full states, merging via a monotonic join-semilattice (commutative, associative, idempotent merge function)
explains Operation-based CRDTs (CmRDT): replicas transmit update operations over causal, reliable broadcast channels
guarantees Strong Eventual Consistency: any two replicas that have received the same set of updates have identical states without conflict negotiation

questions.question: How do Vector Clocks track causal dependencies between distributed database writes and detect concurrent divergent updates?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines a vector clock as an array of logical counters, one per cluster node [V1, V2, ... Vn], attached to each stored version
explains update rule: a node increments its own counter before writing; when receiving updates, it takes component-wise maximums
explains causal comparison: Version A happened-before Version B if every component of V_A <= V_B and at least one is strictly less
explains concurrency detection: if neither vector dominates the other, the writes occurred concurrently and represent a conflict

questions.question: Why are cross-shard joins and distributed aggregations so costly in sharded database architectures, and how are they avoided?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies cost drivers: query router must scatter queries across all shards, transfer massive intermediate datasets over the network, and perform final join in router memory
explains high latency and failure vulnerability: slowest shard (straggler) dictates query response time; memory pressure can crash routing nodes
proposes Table Co-location: sharding related parent-child tables on the same partition key (e.g., customer_id) so joins execute locally on individual nodes
proposes Replicated Reference Tables: broadcasting small, infrequently modified lookup tables (countries, tax rates) to all shard nodes

questions.question: How is distributed Two-Phase Locking implemented across sharded data partitions, and how does distributed deadlock detection operate?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains distributed 2PL: transactions acquire local row/page locks on individual shard nodes where data resides, holding locks until global 2PC completes
identifies distributed deadlock: Transaction T1 on Node A waits for T2, while T2 on Node B waits for T1, creating a circular wait across nodes
describes centralized deadlock detection: nodes send local wait-for graphs to a coordinator, but warns about false alarms (phantom deadlocks) caused by network lag
describes decentralized edge-chasing (Chandy-Misra-Haas) or timestamp abort policies (Wound-Wait/Wait-Die)

questions.question: What is the dual-write problem between a relational database and a message broker, and how does the Transactional Outbox pattern solve it?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: identifies dual-write vulnerability: updating a database and publishing an event to Kafka in separate operations cannot be done atomically without 2PC
describes failure modes: DB commit succeeds but broker publish fails (message lost), or broker publish succeeds but DB commit rolls back (ghost event)
explains Outbox pattern: business entity and event message are written in the SAME local database transaction into an `outbox` table
describes delivery: a background poller or log-tailing CDC processor (Debezium) reads outbox table and reliably publishes to Kafka with at-least-once guarantees

questions.question: Compare the Saga pattern with Two-Phase Commit for distributed microservices in terms of latency, lock holding, and failure recovery.
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains 2PC provides strict ACID guarantees by holding database locks across all nodes until global commit, causing terrible latency and blocking risks
explains Saga pattern breaks a distributed transaction into a sequence of local ACID transactions, committing each immediately without holding distributed locks
describes Saga failure recovery: executes explicit compensating transactions (semantic undo) in reverse order to restore consistency
highlights the critical trade-off: Saga sacrifices Isolation (ACID 'I') because intermediate states are visible to concurrent transactions

questions.question: How are Global Secondary Indexes maintained across a sharded database cluster, and what are the trade-offs between synchronous update and eventual consistency?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: contrasts LSI vs GSI: LSI partitions index with the base table shard key; GSI partitions index on a completely different attribute, scattering index entries across nodes
analyzes synchronous GSI maintenance: every write to a base table requires a distributed 2PC transaction across the base shard and GSI shard, severely penalizing write latency
analyzes asynchronous GSI maintenance (DynamoDB/Cassandra): base table commits immediately, CDC stream updates GSI asynchronously, achieving high write throughput but exposing stale index reads
evaluates operational risks: index lookups returning stale pointers or phantom records during asynchronous replication lag

questions.question: How does the Multi-Paxos consensus algorithm ensure distributed write-ahead log replication across database replicas?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains Basic Paxos flaw: requires 2 round-trips (Phase 1 and Phase 2) for every single consensus decision (log entry)
explains Multi-Paxos optimization: elects a stable Leader via Phase 1 once for thousands of log instances, bypassing Phase 1 for subsequent writes
describes the fast write path: Leader directly executes Phase 2 (Accept -> Accepted) with a majority quorum, achieving single round-trip log commit
explains log hole handling and recovery when a leader crashes and a new leader takes over

questions.question: How does the Raft consensus algorithm manage leader election, log replication, and commit safety in distributed SQL engines?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: describes Leader Election: randomized election timers prevent split votes; Candidate requests votes; majority quorum elects Leader for a given Term
describes Log Replication: Leader receives client command, appends to local log, sends AppendEntries RPC to followers; commits entry once majority replicates
explains Log Matching Invariant: if two logs contain an entry with same index and term, logs are identical up to that index
explains Multi-Raft in distributed SQL (CockroachDB/TiDB): splits data into thousands of ranges, each running an independent Raft consensus group

questions.question: How does log-based Change Data Capture stream low-latency data modifications from the database WAL to downstream search and analytics engines?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: contrasts with polling: polling queries (WHERE updated_at > t) miss intermediate deletes, impose heavy database CPU load, and suffer latency
explains WAL-based CDC: tails the database transaction write-ahead log directly (e.g. PostgreSQL logical decoding slots, MySQL binlog)
highlights zero query overhead: does not execute SELECT queries or acquire table read locks on base tables
describes stream delivery: transforms raw binary row deltas (before/after images) into structured JSON/Avro events emitted to Kafka

questions.question: What is monotonic read consistency in distributed storage, and what client session routing guarantees it when reading from asynchronous replicas?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines monotonic reads: guarantees that if a client reads value V1 at time T1, subsequent reads by the same client will never observe an older value V0
identifies anomaly: Client reads from Replica A (lag 50ms) and sees new post; client refreshes and load balancer routes to Replica B (lag 500ms), making post vanish
describes sticky session routing: hashing user ID to bind a client's queries to a specific replica node
describes version tracking: client maintains a minimum vector clock or LSN cookie, requiring replicas to wait until their apply state catches up before answering

questions.question: What is the precise theoretical and practical distinction between Linearizability and Serializability in distributed database systems?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Serializability: a multi-operation, multi-object transaction property guaranteeing that concurrent execution is equivalent to some serial order, with NO real-time constraint
defines Linearizability: a single-operation, single-object real-time recency guarantee (if write completes at t1, all reads starting at t2 > t1 must observe that write)
explains that a Serializable system can legitimately return stale data from days ago as long as the serial schedule remains logically valid
defines Strict Serializability (External Consistency): combines both guarantees, delivering the strongest possible correctness in distributed databases

questions.question: What is the distributed write skew anomaly in multi-datacenter snapshot isolation, and how do systems enforce global serializability?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains that in multi-datacenter setups, transactions read local snapshots and commit disjoint updates on different datacenters simultaneously
shows that because neither update modified the other's row key, local conflict detectors pass both transactions, violating global business invariants
explains Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI): tracks read-write dependencies dynamically using SIREAD locks / rw-antidependency flags
explains cycle detection: aborts the younger transaction if a dangerous structure (two consecutive rw-antidependencies in the serialization graph) is detected

questions.question: How do modern analytical query engines combine SIMD vector instructions with Blocked Bloom Filters during distributed hash joins?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains runtime filtering: during the build phase of a hash join, coordinator constructs a Bloom filter and broadcasts it to all probe worker nodes
explains pre-filtering benefit: workers evaluate Bloom filter on disk pages or column chunks, discarding non-matching tuples before network shuffle
identifies standard Bloom filter flaw: hashing across a large bit array causes multiple random L3 cache misses per tuple
explains Blocked Bloom Filter: partitions the filter into 64-byte blocks (cache line size); an entire block is loaded and probed with 256-bit AVX2/AVX-512 SIMD instructions in parallel

questions.question: Contrast Crash Fault Tolerant consensus models with Byzantine Fault Tolerant protocols in distributed data systems.
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains CFT assumption (Raft/Paxos): nodes may crash, restart, or delay messages, but never lie, forge digital signatures, or send conflicting votes
states CFT threshold: can tolerate F failures with 2F + 1 nodes (simple majority quorum)
explains BFT assumption (PBFT/Tendermint): nodes may be malicious, compromised, or adversarial, actively sending conflicting messages to deceive the cluster
states BFT threshold: requires 3F + 1 nodes and cryptographic signatures with multiple voting phases (Prepare, Commit) to tolerate F malicious nodes

questions.question: Demonstrate why a given set of functional dependencies can have multiple distinct minimal covers, and explain the implications for schema design.
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: provides a concrete set of dependencies with multiple covers (e.g. {A -> B, B -> A, B -> C, A -> C})
shows that eliminating A -> C yields one minimal cover, whereas replacing B -> C with A -> C yields another equally valid minimal cover
explains that the elimination order of extraneous attributes and redundant dependencies determines the resulting canonical cover
explains the engineering consequence: relational synthesis algorithms (like 3NF synthesis) can produce different schema decompositions depending on the chosen cover

questions.question: How do large-scale distributed databases execute zero-downtime resharding of a high-throughput live table from N shards to 2N shards?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: Phase 1 (Backfill): provision new destination shards and stream historical snapshot data from source shards without interrupting writes
Phase 2 (Catch-up CDC): stream ongoing WAL deltas from source shards to destination shards using CDC to close the replication lag
Phase 3 (Dual-Routing / Verification): router mirrors write traffic or destination shards verify checksum consistency against source shards
Phase 4 (Atomic Switchover): router atomically updates its routing table to direct reads and writes to new shards, followed by decommissioning old shards

questions.question: How does Google's Percolator protocol implement decentralized, snapshot-isolated ACID transactions on top of Bigtable?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains metadata columns: data:t, lock:t, write:t stored per cell in Bigtable, coordinated by a central Timestamp Oracle (TSO)
explains Prewrite Phase: client acquires locks on all modified cells; designates ONE cell as the Primary Lock and points all Secondary Locks to it
explains Commit Phase: client commits the Primary Lock first; once primary lock is converted to a write record, the transaction is irrevocably committed
explains Rollback/Recovery: any client encountering a stranded lock inspects the primary lock cell; if primary committed, client rolls forward the secondary; otherwise aborts

questions.question: How do distributed databases repair stale data replicas using Read Repair during client queries versus background Merkle tree Anti-Entropy repairs?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains Read Repair: during a client read quorum, the coordinator compares data versions returned by replicas; if a replica is stale, an asynchronous write updates it
identifies Read Repair limitation: only repairs keys that are actively queried by clients, leaving cold/dormant records permanently out of sync
explains Anti-Entropy repair: background process that builds hierarchical hash trees (Merkle trees) over key ranges across replicas
shows how Merkle trees compare gigabytes of data by comparing tree root hashes, drilling down only into divergent leaf subtrees to stream missing keys

questions.question: Why is creating a new physical database connection per incoming HTTP request an anti-pattern, and what role does a connection pool play?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains connection overhead: establishing a connection requires TCP 3-way handshake, TLS cryptographic handshake, authentication, and backend process/thread allocation
identifies resource exhaustion: thousands of concurrent HTTP requests spawn thousands of database connections, causing Out-Of-Memory and CPU context-switching thrashing
defines a connection pool as maintaining a warm set of pre-established, reusable connections
describes client borrow/return lifecycle: borrowing an active connection, executing queries, and returning it to the pool for reuse

questions.question: What is the rule of thumb formula for sizing a database connection pool, and why is setting pool size to thousands of connections counter-productive?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: presents the canonical sizing formula: connections = (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count
explains why thousands of connections hurt throughput: a server with 16 CPU cores cannot execute 1,000 threads simultaneously; it wastes CPU cycles on context switching
shows that fewer connections matching hardware parallelism queue requests efficiently in memory, maximizing sustained TPS and reducing latency
connects disk wait states: the extra factor of 2 accounts for threads stalled on disk I/O while another executes on CPU

questions.question: What is the difference between database encryption in transit and encryption at rest?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Encryption in Transit: encrypts network packets between client application and database using TLS/SSL to prevent eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks
defines Encryption at Rest (TDE): encrypts underlying database data files, log files, and backups on persistent storage (disks/SSDs)
identifies attack vectors countered by TDE: protects against stolen physical drives or compromised backup snapshots
notes that TDE decrypts pages transparently when loaded into database buffer RAM, meaning in-memory data requires OS security protections

questions.question: How do Recovery Point Objective and Recovery Time Objective define disaster recovery requirements for databases?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Recovery Point Objective (RPO): the maximum acceptable age of data that can be lost when unexpected downtime occurs (acceptable data loss measured in time)
defines Recovery Time Objective (RTO): the maximum acceptable duration of time the database system can remain offline before restoration (acceptable downtime)
connects RPO to replication: RPO = 0 requires synchronous replication, while asynchronous replication has non-zero RPO matching replication lag
connects RTO to failover automation: manual backup restoration has high RTO (hours); automated multi-region failover achieves low RTO (seconds)

questions.question: What is the distinction between the TPC-C and TPC-H industry benchmarks in evaluating database performance?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines TPC-C: industry standard benchmark for Online Transaction Processing (OLTP), simulating complete wholesale supplier order processing (short read/write transactions, locks, concurrent updates)
defines TPC-H: industry standard benchmark for Online Analytical Processing (OLAP) and Decision Support Systems (DSS), consisting of 22 complex analytical queries (large scans, joins, aggregations)
contrasts metric: TPC-C measures transactions per minute (tpmC) and latency; TPC-H measures composite query throughput over scale factors
explains how storage engines optimize for one versus the other (row stores for TPC-C, columnar stores for TPC-H)

questions.question: What is a vector embedding in modern database systems, and how does similarity search differ from traditional relational keyword search?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines vector embedding as an array of floating-point numbers generated by machine learning models representing semantic meaning in high-dimensional space
contrasts exact match: relational databases filter on discrete equality (=) or range (<, >) predicates using B+ trees
explains similarity search: finds the K nearest neighbor vectors in geometric space based on angular distance or distance metrics
shows how vector search finds semantically identical concepts even when zero exact keyword overlaps exist (e.g. 'automobile' matches 'car')

questions.question: What is the mathematical difference between Cosine Similarity and Euclidean Distance when comparing vector embeddings?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines Euclidean Distance (L2): measures the straight-line physical geometric distance between two coordinate endpoints in N-dimensional space
defines Cosine Similarity: measures the cosine of the angle between two vectors, strictly evaluating orientation and semantic direction regardless of magnitude
explains magnitude invariance: Cosine similarity ignores vector length (useful when text length influences embedding norm)
proves that for normalized unit vectors (magnitude = 1), Cosine Similarity and Euclidean Distance produce identical relative nearest-neighbor rankings

questions.question: Why must database schema migrations always be backward-compatible with currently running application versions?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains rolling deployments: during deployment, old application instances (v1) and new application instances (v2) run concurrently against the same live database
identifies the catastrophe: if a migration deletes or renames a column immediately, running v1 instances instantly crash with SQL errors
explains rule: database changes must support both the currently deployed application and the upcoming version
advocates multi-step decoupled releases over single destructive migrations

questions.question: What is a Block Range Index (BRIN) in PostgreSQL, and for what data ingestion patterns is it vastly smaller and faster than a B+ tree?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: defines BRIN: stores only the minimum and maximum value for ranges of physical disk pages (e.g. 128 pages per block range)
explains how it filters: skips reading entire block ranges if the query predicate falls outside the recorded min/max values
identifies ideal workloads: append-only tables where column values naturally correlate with physical storage order (e.g. created_at timestamps, sequential auto-increment IDs)
compares footprint: a BRIN index is often megabytes compared to gigabytes for an equivalent B+ tree on a 100-million row table

questions.question: How does the principle of least privilege apply to database user accounts used by application microservices?
questions.subject: DBMS
criteria: explains rule: application microservices must never connect as administrative users (e.g. postgres, root, or db_owner)
recommends restricting permissions: grant only required DML commands (SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE) on specific tables, strictly denying DDL (DROP, ALTER)
explains blast radius mitigation: if SQL injection or credentials are leaked, an attacker cannot drop tables, read password hashes, or execute OS shell commands
advocates separate migration service accounts with elevated DDL rights running only during CI/CD deployment pipelines
